name: Gospel
def: Sacred African American vocal music of call-and-response, ecstatic melisma, and church-band backing — the vocal and emotional source of soul and R&B.

traits.v: Melismatic, impassioned lead answered by a congregational choir.
Hand-clap backbeat over a swung 12/8 church feel.
Plagal amen cadences and bluesy added sevenths.
The Black church as performance and community space.

why: Its full-throated melismatic lead and call-and-response exchange are the vocal blueprint soul and R&B inherited wholesale.

tracks.why: Her overdriven electric gospel guitar directly prefigures rock lead playing.

tempoNote: Highly variable — spans slow devotional ballads to uptempo shout numbers.

name: Blues
def: The foundational African American form of the early 1900s — 12-bar I–IV–V harmony, blue notes, and call-and-response that underpin nearly all popular music to follow.

traits.v: 12-bar I–IV–V with flattened blue thirds and sevenths.
Bent, vocalised blue notes and call-and-response phrasing.
Three-line AAB verse over a repeating 12-bar cycle.
Southern Black work-song and vaudeville roots.

why: The 12-bar cycle and bent blue notes set a harmonic and expressive grammar that rock, soul and R&B all build on.
tempoNote: Wide range — slow blues to uptempo shuffles.

name: Delta Blues
def: The raw, rural Mississippi root of blues — solo voice and slide or fingerpicked guitar, bent notes and a haunted, percussive drive.

traits.v: Loose, percussive solo-guitar drive, often free of strict meter.
Sparse one- to three-chord blues anchored on the I chord.
Buzzing bottleneck slide and overdriven acoustic tone.

why: Bottleneck slide and bent blue notes over a single droning chord set the expressive vocabulary all blues guitar grew from.

albums.t: King of the Delta Blues Singers

tracks.why: The bent thirds and slide became the DNA of rock lead guitar.

tempoNote: Often loose or free of strict meter — treat as approximate.

name: Chicago Blues
def: Delta blues electrified and urbanised — amplified guitar and harmonica, a full rhythm section, and a louder, band-driven sound built for city clubs.

traits.v: Amplified guitar and harp, bass, drums, piano.
Overdriven amp grit and reverb-soaked harmonica.
Heavy shuffle and an insistent backbeat.

why: Plugging the Delta into an amplifier produced the distorted, sustaining guitar tone that rock would push further.

name: Rhythm & Blues
def: Electrified, urban, and groove-forward — blues amplified with a backbeat, horns, and dancefloor intent. The pivot from rural lament to city celebration.

traits.v: Strong backbeat and a danceable shuffle.
Electric guitar, piano, and punchy horn sections.
Shouting, gospel-tinged lead delivery.

why: It gives the blues a backbeat, horns and amplification, turning lament into urban dance music.

tracks.why: Its driving backbeat is the literal template rock 'n' roll copied.

name: Soul
def: Gospel fervour secularised — the raw, melismatic church voice applied to love and life over tight R&B bands.

traits.v: Gospel-derived melisma, ad-libs and call-and-response with horns.
Tight backbeat, syncopated bass, punchy horn stabs.
1960s Black pride and the civil-rights era.

why: It transplants gospel's ecstatic vocal phrasing onto secular song, keeping the church's call-and-response interplay.

albums.t: I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You

tracks.t: (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay

name: Funk
def: Rhythm stripped to 'the One' — interlocking syncopated guitar, bass and drums prioritising groove and repetition over chord change.

traits.v: Syncopated sixteenth-note interlock locked to a strong downbeat.
Static one- or two-chord vamps.
Slap bass, clipped wah guitar, tight horns.
Open, vamp-based jams rather than verse-chorus.

why: Everything serves a repeating syncopated groove anchored on the first beat, harmony frozen so rhythm can dominate.

tracks.why: The locked one-chord vamp is the rhythmic cell funk and much dance music spin from.

tracks.t: Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin)

name: Philadelphia Soul
def: Soul made lush and orchestral in Philadelphia — Gamble & Huff and Thom Bell's sweeping strings, horns and vibraphone over a smooth, gliding rhythm section, cut at Sigma Sound for Philadelphia International.

traits.v: Full string and horn sections, vibraphone and glockenspiel over a soul rhythm section.
Smooth, steady, hi-hat-driven groove that edges toward four-on-the-floor.
Sweet falsetto leads and close vocal-group harmony beside gruff baritone testifying.
House-band studio sound — MFSB at Sigma Sound, arranged and producer-led.
Philadelphia International Records, early-to-mid 1970s.

why: It trades southern soul's grit for symphonic polish, and its MFSB house band's steady, string-laden groove is the sound disco was built from.

tracks.why: The Soul Train theme: a strings-and-hi-hat instrumental that sits right on the line between Philly soul and disco.

tracks.t: If You Don't Know Me by Now

name: Disco
def: Four-on-the-floor dance music born in queer, Black and Latino clubs — lush orchestration, syncopated bass and the 12-inch extended mix.

traits.v: Four-on-the-floor kick under syncopated octave bass.
String and horn sections, wah guitar, early synths.
Extended 12-inch arrangements for the DJ.
Dancefloor, peak-time.

why: It puts a steady four-on-the-floor kick under funk's syncopation and lush orchestration, built for the extended club mix.

tracks.why: Moroder's all-synth arpeggio pointed straight at the machine-made future of dance music.

name: Spirituals & Work Songs
def: African American spirituals and work songs — communal, a cappella call-and-response born in slavery, the field and the church, and the deepest root of gospel, blues and jazz.

traits.v: Communal call-and-response, frequently a cappella.
A labour pulse of hand-claps and foot-stomps.
The plantation, field and church of the 19th-century South.

why: Communal call-and-response sung over a labour pulse is the ancestral cell from which gospel, blues and jazz all descend.

name: Boogie-Woogie
def: A rolling, up-tempo blues piano style built on a repeating walking-bass ostinato — raucous, percussive and made for dancing.

traits.v: A repeating eight-to-the-bar walking-bass ostinato.
Percussive, driving, two-fisted piano.
Rent-party and dancehall.

why: Its rolling eight-to-the-bar bass became the engine of jump blues, R&B and early rock 'n' roll piano.

name: Future Funk
def: A sample-based revival that speeds up and chops disco, funk and Japanese city-pop into glossy, nostalgic dance loops — a streaming-era descendant of disco by way of vaporwave.

traits.v: Sped-up, filtered samples of disco, funk and city-pop.
Four-on-the-floor bounce under chopped vocal cuts.
Online, meme- and anime-adjacent net-label culture.

why: It rebuilds disco and funk from sped-up, filtered samples, extending the dancefloor into vaporwave-era internet nostalgia.

tracks.why: Its chopped, sped-up disco sample is the future-funk formula in miniature.

name: Psychedelic Soul
def: Soul wired through the psychedelic studio — wah and fuzz guitar, echo, long-form arrangements and social commentary over gospel-rooted vocals.

traits.v: Wah and fuzz guitar, phasing and studio echo over soul rhythm sections.
Extended, multi-part productions beyond the 3-minute single.
Late-60s Black pop responding to psychedelia and social upheaval.

why: Producers like Norman Whitfield ran Motown's vocal-group formula through rock's effects rack and lengthened the groove into a trip.

tracks.why: Whitfield wiring wah, echo and social realism into the Motown machine.

name: Deep Funk
def: Raw, regional funk 45s — small labels, live-in-the-room drums and open breaks; the crate-digger's funk that later fed hip-hop's sample banks.

traits.v: Hard, unquantised drum breaks left open in the arrangement.
Lo-fi, live-to-tape small-studio grit.
Regional 45 scenes — New Orleans, Memphis, the chitlin circuit.

why: Away from major-label polish, small bands cut groove-first singles whose open drum breaks became sampling's raw material.

tracks.why: Its strutting break is one of the most sampled grooves ever cut.

name: Psychedelic Funk
def: Funk's locked groove stretched into acid-rock space — screaming fuzz leads, studio effects and cosmic theatrics over 'the One'.

traits.v: Overdriven fuzz guitar and synth squall over funk rhythm sections.
Long-form jams and concept-album sprawl.
Post-Hendrix Black rock — Funkadelic, post-Riot Sly.

why: Funkadelic put Hendrix's guitar language on top of James Brown's rhythm section and refused to choose between them.

albums.t: Free Your Mind... and Your Ass Will Follow

tracks.why: A ten-minute fuzz-guitar elegy over a funk band — the fusion in one track.

tracks.t: If I'm in Luck I Might Get Picked Up

name: Library Funk
def: Production-music funk cut for film and TV libraries — KPM, De Wolfe and Bruton session players writing tight, mood-labelled grooves never meant for the charts.

traits.v: Licensed library LPs for broadcast use, anonymous session elite.
Punchy, clean-cut breaks engineered to sit under dialogue.
Short cues by mood — 30 seconds to 3 minutes.

why: Written to order and pressed obscure, its pristine breaks and horn stabs resurfaced decades later as prime sampling material.

tracks.why: A library cue that ended up in trailers, turntables and hip-hop records alike.

tempoNote: Variable — production cues span moods by design.

name: Cosmic Disco
def: The Italian lakeside answer to disco — DJs pitching records down into a slow, hypnotic, synth-heavy churn that mixed disco with krautrock, African and dub records.

traits.v: Slow, rolling tempos far below disco’s peak-time pulse.
Late-70s Italian clubs — Baldelli at Cosmic, Loda at Typhoon.
Hypnosis over euphoria — the long blend as instrument.

why: By playing disco at the wrong speed and mixing in anything electronic or African, cosmic DJs invented a slower, weirder dancefloor.

tracks.why: Synth disco the cosmic DJs pitched down into slow-motion hypnosis.

name: Doo-Wop
def: R&B vocal-group harmony from the street corners of New York, Philadelphia and Chicago: nonsense-syllable backing voices, a bass anchor and a falsetto lead over I–vi–IV–V changes.

traits.v: Falsetto or tenor lead over blended backing voices and a bass singer.
The I–vi–IV–V "50s progression", often in a slow 12/8.
Voices first; sparse piano, guitar and a soft backbeat.
Street-corner rehearsal and small independent R&B labels.

why: It fixed the chord changes and the falsetto slow-dance ballad that Spector, Orbison and every retro-noir act since have reused.

tracks.why: A 1954 independent single that crossed to the pop chart and set the slow I–vi–IV–V ballad template.

tracks.t: I Only Have Eyes for You
In the Still of the Night

tempoNote: Two speeds — slow 12/8 ballads and up-tempo jump numbers.
